material_units.source_text:
Fact — Deterministic loops on finite state spaces cycle
      
        If $X$ is finite and $x_{t+1}=F(x_t)$ for a fixed $F:X\to X$ (stationary deterministic feedback and dynamics), every state the trajectory ever visits appears among $x_0,\dots,x_{|X|-1}$; so if it ever enters a failure set, it does so by time $|X|-1$.
        Proof. The $|X|+1$ states $x_0,\dots,x_{|X|}$ lie in a set of size $|X|$, so $x_i=x_j$ for some $0\le i\lt j\le|X|$ (pigeonhole). Determinism gives $x_{i+m}=x_{j+m}$ for all $m\ge0$ (induction on $m$), so from time $i$ on the trajectory repeats $x_i,\dots,x_{j-1}$, and $j-1\le|X|-1$. $\blacksquare$
hypotheses: An arbitrary finite state type and an actual sequence with x(n+1)=F(x(n)) for one fixed deterministic map F.
The existence of the sequence supplies a state x(0), so the state cardinality is positive. No empty-state horizon is silently used.
The failure set is arbitrary. The result does not apply to changing maps, unrecorded controller state or stochastic transitions.

material_units.source_text:
Definition — Principle of mathematical induction
      
        If $P(0)$ is true (base case) and $P(t)\Rightarrow P(t+1)$ for every $t\in\mathbb N$ (induction step), then $P(t)$ holds for all $t\in\mathbb N$. In strong induction the step may use all of $P(0),\dots,P(t)$.
hypotheses: An arbitrary proposition P over natural-number indices.
The ordinary principle assumes P(0) and P(n)->P(n+1). The strong principle assumes all k<n when proving P(n), equivalently all indices through t when proving P(t+1).
material_units.per_unit_reason: Read the full definition parent. Both the ordinary base/successor principle and the strong earlier-case variant match the genuine arbitrary-proposition induction theorems.
